Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

# Sparse diagonal stroke continuation

## When to use
Use when an ARC grid has a mostly uniform background and compact sparse motifs that may encode diagonal lines extended to grid boundaries. This is a class-level hypothesis workflow, not an ID-specific answer recipe.

## Workflow
1. Record all non-background coordinates and group by color. Separate same-color aligned pairs/segments from isolated cells and from mixed-color diagonal chains.
2. For each plausible same-color segment, test both diagonal orientations (down-right/up-left and down-left/up-right). Identify segment endpoints and compute exact ray cells to boundaries without altering the seed.
3. Compare each prediction against every demo output. Record which colors/segments extend, which directions fire, and which plausible near-matches are unchanged. Do not infer that every diagonal pair activates.
4. Apply only the demonstrated selector and ray paths to the test. Preserve other cells and seed colors unless outputs explicitly change them. Mechanically validate dimensions and coordinate indices.
5. After incorrect feedback, reject that hypothesis and identify the alternative selector distinction; do not repeat a similar output with minor transcription changes.

- Mixed-color objects can resemble a diagonal run; require same-color evidence unless demos show otherwise.

# task-37f0b9db: Fill gaps between same-line markers

## Verified rule
For each row and each column independently, find consecutive occurrences of the marker color. Recolor every cell strictly between each consecutive pair to color 3. Preserve marker cells and all cells not strictly between consecutive same-line markers. Do not extend beyond the outermost markers. Overlapping row/column fills are simply color 3.

The background is not fixed: it was 9 in the demo and 1 in the verified test. Marker color likewise varied: 1 in the demo and 7 in the test. Identify marker cells by the prominent sparse non-background color; output fill color was 3 in both.

## Evidence and validation
Demo (10x11): background 9, markers 1. Output inserted 3 only in row/column gaps. Examples: row 1 between markers at columns 4 and 9 filled c5–8; column 0 between markers at rows 5 and 9 filled r6–8; column 9 between markers at rows 1 and 5 filled r2–4. Markers and other cells unchanged.

Verified test (28x11): background 1, markers 7; the test output was accepted. Apply gap filling separately to every row/column pair of consecutive 7s, using 3. Isolated marker(s) on a line don't trigger fills; never bridge past endpoints or fill whole lines.

## Pitfalls
- Do not treat background as necessarily 0 or hardcode demo background 9.
- Do not extend rays outward from marker pairs; fill only the bounded intervals between consecutive markers.
- Keep all marker-color cells unchanged even where horizontal and vertical intervals intersect elsewhere.
- Row and column operations are both required and can overlap."
}
